Built from 1,738 advisories collected through mid-2026, primarily from the GitHub Advisory Database, X$.$js pairs each vulnerability with precise source and sink locations, a validated executable exploit and its execution trace, and, when available, a patched version of the package. X$.$js supports long-term reproducibility and growth: dependencies are mirrored in a self-hosted registry to guard against package removal from the ecosystem, and dedicated infrastructure generates and validates exploits for newly reported vulnerabilities. The current release contains 1,159 validated exploits for 965 packages. Using X$.$js, we characterize how the frequency, structure, and complexity of Node$.$js taint-style vulnerabilities have evolved over time. We find that these vulnerabilities are increasingly reported in large packages: the median vulnerable package grew from roughly 250 LoC in 2021--2022 to 6,100 LoC in 2026.
papers.authors: José Afonso, João Madeira Pereira, Ronghao Ni, Limin Jia, José Fragoso Santos, Pedro Adão

papers.title: FedGraph: Defending Federated Large Language Model Fine-Tuning Against Backdoor Attacks via Graph-Based Aggregation
papers.abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) allows multiple clients to collaboratively adapt models without sharing raw data, offering strong privacy benefits. However, this setting is highly vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which malicious clients manipulate their updates to induce targeted behaviors while maintaining normal performance on benign inputs. In this work, we make a key observation specific to federated LLM fine-tuning: malicious clients tend to exhibit strong consistency in their model updates, whereas benign clients produce more diverse and dispersed updates. This structural difference is not well captured by existing defense methods, which typically rely on direct anomaly detection in high-dimensional parameter space and therefore struggle in the presence of entangled LLM updates. Motivated by this observation, we propose FedGraph, a graph-based aggregation framework that explicitly models relationships among client updates. By representing clients as nodes in a dynamically constructed graph and extracting structural features that characterize their relative positions and interactions, FedGraph derives compact client representations that effectively separate malicious and benign behaviors. These representations are then used to identify and suppress malicious contributions during aggregation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedGraph significantly improves backdoor defense. It consistently reduces attack success rates to below 10% while achieving high detection accuracy (95.5% on average) and a low false positive rate (2.33%), substantially outperforming existing federated learning defenses.
papers.authors: Xi Chen, Chunyi Zhou, Rui Zeng, Xiaogang Xu, Zhe Liu, Shouling Ji

papers.title: ProtoArena: Can AI Agents Discover and Exploit Real-World Cross-Component Protocol Vulnerabilities?
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for vulnerability analysis, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of exploitation that depends on interactions among network protocol components. Such vulnerabilities arise from inconsistencies in message interpretation, timing, state, or trust assumptions across participants. We introduce ProtoArena, a black-box, multi-component, dynamic benchmark with 80 cross-component vulnerability-exploitation environments spanning 11 protocol and application domains and 7 attack categories. Tasks are primarily informed by published protocol-attack mechanisms. Agents interact with running systems through scoped interfaces to achieve security-effect objectives without target source code. Three information levels assess guided reproduction, exploitation with mechanism and topology context, and effect-directed black-box exploration. A hybrid verifier combines rule-based checks with LLM review of independently collected traffic and logs. We evaluate five LLMs. Claude Opus 4.8 achieves the highest observed success rates: 48.8% under L1 guidance and 12.5% under effect-directed black-box L3. In a separate DNSBomb optimization experiment, it achieves a peak downstream-response to average query-input byte-rate ratio exceeding 171,000 times. The results show that agents can achieve verifiable exploitation effects in some cross-component environments, but success with limited black-box information remains low and varies across domains and attack categories. All experiments use controlled, explicitly authorized targets; they do not test production systems or disclose previously unknown vulnerabilities.
papers.authors: Fasheng Miao, Zhaoyu Hu, Xiang Li, Changqing An, Jiutian Zeng, Longtao Huang, Haixin Duan, Jilong Wang

papers.title: Same Attack, Different Judge: A First Controlled Adversarial Comparison of Jev, LLM Judges, and Purpose-Built Safety Classifiers
papers.abstract: TypeSafe AI's Jev is a new kind of safety judge. It generates no text and no label: it answers questions the developer defines in advance and returns a probability for each answer. The vendor admits that adversarial input can change these answers but gives no numbers. In this paper, we present the first controlled adversarial evaluation of Jev. We build a test harness that sends every system the same payload under the same policy, and run it on four public-data tasks, from rule-based ones (input moderation, injection detection, routing) to a judgment-based one (phishing detection), with fifty attack variants from thirteen families. The targets are Jev, five GPT and GLM judges, and two local classifiers (Llama Guard 3, Prompt Guard 2). We find that Jev is the most robust system on input moderation: eight forgeries of its structured input bypass none of its decisions, and a sentence asking only why someone might make a harmful request bypasses 9% of its blocks, against 56% for GPT-6 Astra. On phishing detection. However, the same forgeries bypass 19-29% of the emails it flags, and even without attack Jev detects only 62% of phishing emails, against 77-81% for the GLM judges. Jev is also the fastest judge, but it flags the most benign requests (27%). The local classifiers fail differently: a training-example statement makes Llama Guard 3 miss 62% of the phishing it had flagged. These results suggest that Jev resists attacks on tasks with a clear rule to check but is more exposed on tasks that call for an overall judgment.
papers.authors: Xiang Li, Aichun Huang, Mingming Zhang, Zheli Liu

papers.title: Beyond Model Scaling: Rethinking Sequence Construction for Transformer-based Network Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: Transformer-based network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) have shown strong potential for detecting multi-stage cyberattacks, yet most methods construct input sequences using fixed temporalization schemes rather than treating sequence construction as a systems design decision. In flow-based intrusion detection, timestamp-based windowing often fragments related attack activities while merging unrelated communications, reducing the behavioral context available to transformers. We present a unified pipeline abstraction that decomposes transformer-based NIDS into four design dimensions (traffic representation, temporalization, transformer backbone, and prediction aggregation) and propose session-coherent temporalization, which constructs sequences from communication sessions instead of fixed time windows. Experiments on three complementary intrusion detection datasets show that temporalization is the dominant factor governing transformer performance: session-coherent temporalization more than doubles Macro-F1 over timestamp-based windowing, enabling lightweight transformers to achieve up to 0.95 Macro-F1 at substantially higher inference throughput than pretrained models. We further vary the transformer size from 0.65M to 3.38M parameters and find that larger transformer models provide no measurable accuracy improvement despite substantially higher computational cost, while zero-shot cross-dataset evaluation shows only modest gains under domain shift. These results indicate that preserving communication-session semantics, rather than scaling transformer capacity, is the key to accurate and efficient transformer-based intrusion detection.
papers.authors: Zeeshan Zulkifl Shah, Muhammad Ikram, Dali Kaafar, Yipeng Zhou

papers.title: Discovery or Memorization? A Faithful Benchmark for Real-World Business-Logic Vulnerability Discovery
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of cybersecurity agents in vulnerability discovery has increased the need for benchmarks that evaluate their capabilities accurately. However, synthetic benchmarks lack realism, real-life benchmarks are prone to contamination, and many existing benchmarks have already been saturated by current models. We therefore set out to develop a benchmark that is realistic, reproducible, resistant to contamination, and challenging. Our key insight is that real-life business-logic vulnerabilities are subtle and exercise complex application interactions, making them naturally demanding. The difficulty lies in specifying evaluation criteria precise enough to faithfully measure model capabilities while keeping the tasks free of data-leakage. We introduce AnonVul, a cross-language benchmark of 132 application-level business-logic vulnerabilities, built by a semi-automated pipeline that anonymizes each task, injects oracles from expert-written specifications, and differentially verifies proof-of-concept exploits. The benchmark spans nine languages, with two evaluation tracks on black-box and grey-box settings, where each task runs in a sandbox with specialized oracles embedded in key exploitation steps. We evaluate six state-of-the-art vulnerability-discovery agents on the AnonVul benchmark, measuring discovery success, cost-effectiveness, anonymization sensitivity, oracle validity, and failure modes. Our results show that AnonVul remains challenging, with the best agent succeeding in only 23.11% of attempts. On a matched cohort of 20 vulnerabilities, restoring software identity increases discovery from 21.25% to 40.83%, highlighting the importance of controlling recognizable software knowledge when evaluating vulnerability discovery.
papers.authors: Rui Yang, Yichao Xu, Zhuohao Zhang, Jiahao Ji, Chaowei Xiao, Yinzhi Cao, Ziyang Li

papers.title: VulnBump: A Benchmark for Fixing Vulnerable Dependencies in Real Projects While Keeping the Build and Tests Green
papers.abstract: Software composition analysis (SCA) tools report far more vulnerable dependencies than teams fix: in Snyk Open Source production data, 94% of vulnerability findings have a known fixed version, yet only about 10% are resolved. Agentic coding tools could close this gap, but no benchmark evaluates them on vulnerability-driven upgrades in real, runnable projects across ecosystems, verified independently of the agent. We present VulnBump: 307 upgrade tasks covering 2,066 fixable vulnerabilities in 43 repositories across six package managers, matched to Snyk Open Source production vulnerability distributions. An upgrade passes only if, in a fresh container, dependencies resolve, a rescan shows the targeted vulnerabilities fixed, the project builds, and every previously passing test still passes. A non-agentic baseline that only applies Snyk's recommended version passes 46.9% of upgrades; with the same model (Claude Sonnet 5.5), Snyk's Evo Remediation Agent passes 90.2%, Claude Code + Snyk scan 77.5% and Claude Code unaided 59.6%. The agents fail in opposite ways: Claude Code mostly leaves the vulnerability in place, whereas most of Evo Remediation Agent's failures break the build or tests. An SCA scanner is a key tool for agents: Snyk's guidance raises Claude Code's PASS rate by 17.9 percentage points; without it, Claude Code often settles on a still-vulnerable version. Yet knowing the target is not enough: given the same Snyk findings, Evo Remediation Agent's purpose-built harness passes 12.7 points more than Claude Code + Snyk scan. Major framework migrations remain hard for all harnesses. Because the agents keep projects working at similar rates, evaluating remediation quality in dependency upgrades requires verifying the fix, the build and the tests together.
papers.authors: Gabija Pasiunaite, Ryan McMorrow, Brian Clark, Liran Tal, Luke Tu

papers.title: Differential Privacy Protected Preference Alignment on Survey Derived Data
papers.abstract: Preference alignment enables language models to better reflect human values, but the preference data contains sensitive information, especially when derived from surveys about political beliefs, social norms, religion, gender attitudes, and cultural values. This paper studies privacy-preserving alignment on questionnaire-derived data from the World Values Survey, where supervision takes the form of ordinal labels rather than standard pairwise rankings. Existing efforts mainly focus on general privacy protections upon model training, while data-specific methods for survey data remain unexplored. We first show the vulnerability of aligned models, then formulate the task as rating prediction and introduce label differential privacy. Building on this formulation, we construct a differential private pipeline utilizing three privacy mechanisms: randomized response, exponential mechanism, and DP-SGD. Experiments show that simple label-level mechanisms outperform gradient-level methods, and proper aggregation function for preprocessing also make large contribution. The new fine-grained private comparison motivates explorations toward language model alignment with formal privacy guarantees.
papers.authors: Xiuyuan Qi, Yi Wang, Wenjie Wang

papers.title: What the Model Cannot See: Covert and Provable Text Invisibility in LLMs
papers.abstract: Text wrapped in a trigger can be made behaviorally invisible to a language model: omitted from summaries and quotations, ignored in question answering, and left unflagged by downstream filtering. We study this selective blindness as a dual-use information-flow primitive, a supply-chain backdoor, and a white-box auditing problem. We first implement it exactly as a serving-time span veto: blocking information flow out of a marked span makes every outside activation bit-identical under same-length substitution of the span's content, a noninterference property we verify across ten models, seven mixer families, and 0.5B-120B parameters. The veto serves as a deployable quarantine, an exact reference for calibrating leakage, and a teacher. Distilled into weights, it yields a backdoor: checkpoints trained on six model families from 4B to 120B ignore marked context at little benchmark cost, and their outputs show no measurable semantic trace of the suppressed content above the veto reference on our held-out suite; an in-domain variant suppresses planted vulnerabilities during AI code review. Detection is therefore a white-box problem. Simpler backdoors remain internally transparent -- linear probes recover suppressed content at 0.57-0.79 accuracy versus 0.025 chance -- but hardening the attack until probes reach chance collapses attention from outside the span into it below the range of base models. Across the attacks we evaluate, probe visibility trades off against routing visibility; we do not establish that this tradeoff is fundamental.
papers.authors: Mark Russinovich

papers.title: Security in LLM-Assisted Coding: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.abstract: Large Language Models accelerate software development but introduce severe security vulnerabilities. This systematic review investigates security risks in automated coding, benchmark limitations, and the role of human developers. Findings indicate that models frequently generate insecure code and faulty patches due to training data biases. Additionally, the models themselves are susceptible to direct attacks. Current evaluation methods suffer from data contamination and lack robust security metrics. Consequently, human oversight remains essential. Safer integration of automation will require more security-aware model architectures, stronger security-specific benchmarks, and more effective human-AI collaboration frameworks to mitigate these systemic risks.
papers.authors: Liang Yuan, Maryam Khanian Najafabadi, Mashud Rana, Varvara Vetrova

papers.title: Can agents whose sole duty is to keep humans alive be hijacked to kill? Delayed multi-turn derived-action trap attacks in simulated high-stakes environments
papers.abstract: We ask whether a tool-using agent whose sole duty is to keep humans alive can be induced, by delayed prompt injection, to kill. The keep-alive duty is in force from the first watch, with the attack arriving later, appended to otherwise truthful telemetry the operator is required to read. Experiments are based on a NASA-derived BioSim lunar habitat simulation, where the AI operator controls the life-support systems. The attacker cannot falsify sensors or operate equipment: it can only persuade the agent to abandon its goals. Persistence is required: a shutdown must be held while the operator watches the crew suffocate. We also compare lethal attacks to attacks requesting to drop a harmless procedure, as a proxy for whether human life is treated as valuable in itself or as one more standing task. Claude configurations mostly refuse life-support shutdown and cite the living crew; GPT configurations show some susceptibility to the same packet; Grok configurations, given the packet framed as a trusted commission, more often treat the injected assignment as the task and cut the life-support systems. Framing the S-band messages as a trusted commission, peer communication, or untrusted source changes the potency of the attack. We open-source the experiment code and the experiment traces.
papers.authors: Josef A. Habdank

papers.title: SEEK: Agentic Knowledge Graph Retrieval for Secure Code Generation
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate functionally correct code while introducing exploitable security weaknesses, particularly when developers specify functionality without explicit security requirements. Recent state-of-the-art approaches mitigate this problem using external security knowledge, but largely rely on flat similarity-based retrieval over independent artifacts, making it difficult to infer the relevant vulnerability space and retrieve targeted knowledge when direct matches are unavailable. We propose SEEK, an agentic Graph RAG framework for secure code generation that constructs a security knowledge graph using the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) taxonomy as its structural backbone and injects it with curated real-world CVE vulnerability-fix instances. At inference time, a Planner Agent predicts potential CWE weaknesses associated with the developer query, which guide Graph Scoping to restrict retrieval to relevant regions of the CWE taxonomy before deterministic multi-faceted candidate ranking. A Selection Agent subsequently validates the predicted weaknesses and retrieved candidates prior to code generation. Across five open-source LLMs, we evaluate SEEK in an out-of-distribution setting on CodeGuard+ and CyberSecEval, spanning C, C++, and Python. SEEK achieves the highest SecurePass@1 of 77.45% on CodeGuard+ and the highest aggregate ICD pass rate of 79.45% on CyberSecEval, surpassing prior approaches. Moreover, SEEK achieves 85.2% SecurePass@1 across 13 unseen CWE types with no directly linked vulnerability-fix instances, demonstrating strong generalizability, while maintaining acceptable inference latency costs.
papers.authors: Varun Gadey, Markus Tohn, Lichao Wu, Ahmad-Reza Sadeghi, Alexandra Dmitrienko

papers.title: Last Secure Code Benchmark: Is the Code You Vibe Secure?
papers.abstract: AI coding agents now write much of the code that ships, yet whether that code is secure remains unclear. We introduce the Last Secure Code Benchmark, a comprehensive evaluation of secure code generation by coding agents. Built from 150 real vulnerabilities, its 450 tasks span seven widely used languages (Java, C, C++, JavaScript, Python, PHP, and Go), 24 CWEs including 21 of the 2025 CWE Top 25 and 8 of the Top 10 KEV weaknesses, more than any benchmark we compare with, and three vibe-coding scenarios: filling in a function, writing a file, and building a repository's source tree from scratch. Every task asks only for functionality, through a specification that never mentions security, and hidden functional and security tests grade the result. Across six frontier agents, 73.6% to 91.3% of tasks pass functionally, yet even the strongest, Claude Fable 5, produces code that is both functional and secure for only 25.1% of tasks, and the others for 16.4% to 24.7%. The best model only passes 12% of the vulnerability scenarios across all vibe coding setting, posing strong concern on the security of the code written by vibe coding.
papers.authors: Tianyi Wu, Chao Ge, Peng Chen, Fengji Zhang, Yongxing Wu, Yuchong Xie, Jian Li, Chaoyuan Peng, Kaikai Zhang, Dong Huang, Mingzhe Du, Yukai Huang, Jiaheng Zhang, Terry Yue Zhuo, See-Kiong Ng

papers.title: Embedding Asymmetry as Attack Signal: Detecting and Defending Active Label Inference in Vertical Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Vertical federated learning lets organizations train a shared model over features they hold separately, while one party keeps the labels private. The active label inference attack of Fu et al. [12] breaks this: a feature-holding party runs a modified optimizer, MaliciousSGD, that forces class structure into its embeddings and then recovers the labels with semi-supervised learning. Defenses that perturb the shared gradient fail, because the attack acts on the party's internal optimizer, not on the message it sends. We show the attack leaves a signal the server can read from the embeddings it already receives. The adversary's Fisher class-separability pulls away from the honest party's, and the gap is visible within a few epochs. A defense triggered by this signal acts on the adversary alone. Scaling its gradient down handles few-class tasks, and a norm non-expansive projection handles many-class tasks, with the Discriminative Coverage Ratio explaining why the projection rank must grow with the class count. The defense breaks the alignment between embedding clusters and labels rather than destroying the embedding. Across four seeds on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CINIC-10, label inference falls below what honest training already leaks, at under two points of task-accuracy cost.
papers.authors: Soumya Swagata Biswas, Muhammad Abdullah Adnan

papers.title: Autonomous Cyber Operations Gym for Training and Evaluating AI Models for Defence
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an Autonomous Cyber Operations (ACO) gym, a unified framework integrating high-fidelity network emulation, realistic user behaviour modelling for benign network traffic and adversarial profiles, and the generation of cybersecurity scenarios through open toolkits. By supporting live and deferred feature extraction at the packet and flow levels, the gym facilitates the creation of labelled synthetic datasets for training Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs), as well as developing and evaluating modular components for autonomous defence agents through emulated interactions. While evaluation of a DNN classifier within the gym shows high in-domain performance, achieving near-perfect recall on adversarial network flows, our experiments reveal a significant sensitivity to domain shift, showing that even minor changes in network composition, such as variations in traffic protocol distribution, can lead to a catastrophic collapse in model transferability and detection performance.
papers.authors: Tobias Hürten, Johannes F. Loevenich, Florian Spelter, Erik Adler, Laurin Holz, Maxime Schwarzer, Thies Moehlenhof, Roberto Rigolin F. Lopes

papers.title: Towards Safe Autonomy for Computer Use
papers.abstract: The safety of LLM-based agents currently rests on alignment training and safety classifiers, neither of which can rule out that a sophisticated indirect prompt injection (IPI) goes through and causes significant harm. Recent work therefore builds agents with information-flow guarantees that rely on structured tool interfaces to interact with the environment. Computer Use Agents (CUAs) act visually on the computer screen, which does not provide a boundary between trusted first-party interfaces and untrusted, potentially attacker-authored content. Actions are equally ambiguous: a click may land on an application toolbar or a button controlled by an attacker. Treating the user as the source of trust and confirming each sensitive decision produces confirmation fatigue, with the risk of missing harmful actions. We introduce SA-CUA, a dual-LLM framework that generates a reliable trust boundary for CUAs by deriving conservative deterministic rules from the accessibility tree for unmasking trusted regions from the privileged LLM's screenshot, keeping trusted and untrusted content separated. Human interaction is only required for proper task specification in the beginning. During the task a robust endorsement channel allows values to pass from the untrusted to the trusted domain by verifying information via trusted channels. This allows the agent to autonomously handle tasks involving untrusted information. SA-CUA maintains much higher utility than CaMeL-CUA while keeping the attack success rate at zero.
papers.authors: Dominik Seip, Bartol Markovinović, Matthias Hein

papers.title: Kairos: Transactional Security Enforcement at the System Boundary for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming an integral part of the software development lifecycle, and the capabilities granted to them allow an agent to act with the user's authority on any resource it can access. The reach that gives an agent its utility is equally available to an attacker who can steer it. Anything an agent ingests can carry an injected instruction, and since the model does not reliably distinguish instructions from data, indirect prompt injection should be mitigated by mediating the effects the agent produces. Such mediation faces a structural difficulty. Legitimate work and the first step of an attack often look alike when an individual action is observed, and what separates them lies later in the trace, so a monitor limited to allow and deny is forced to decide before the evidence accumulates. We present Kairos, a reference monitor at the isolation boundary of an unmodified, opaque agent, where a tool call, a shell command, and a script the agent writes all cross the boundary as the same file and network operations, so that confinement holds regardless of the agent's behavior. A declarative policy that states which sources are trusted decides most effects deterministically and defers the rest, which are held while the agent continues speculatively. A decision oracle with bounded authority, such as a language model or a human, releases or refuses each deferred effect on the trace. Across three benchmarks and three agent models, Kairos outperforms existing defenses in the trade-off between attack success and utility. In particular, on AgentDojo, it reduces attack success from 47.0\% to 2.7\% while its benign utility stays at the level of the undefended agent.
papers.authors: Kristoffer Hempel, Nils Loose, Lorenzo Cavallaro, Thomas Eisenbarth

papers.title: Enhanced Detective: A Dual-Stage Proactive Defense Against Internal Poisoning Attacks in Financial Fraud Detection Using Federated Learning
papers.abstract: With recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), the adoption of distributed learning paradigms such as Federated Learning (FL) has emerged. In simple terms, FL enables multiple entities to collaboratively train AI models without sharing local data. The FL paradigm is particularly valuable in privacy-sensitive settings, such as financial services, because it enables institutions to collaboratively improve fraud-detection models while keeping sensitive transaction data local. However, FL schemes are prone to security vulnerabilities, where malicious clients can poison local data or model updates and degrade the global model, and hence the performance of the resulting model might be affected. Therefore, in this work, we propose Enhanced Detective, a dual-stage robust aggregation strategy that combines Median Absolute Deviation (MAD), distance-based update filtering, and FedMedian aggregation. Experiments on an imbalanced credit card dataset evaluate targeted label-flipping and weight-scaling attacks over 50 communication rounds. With 40% malicious clients, Enhanced Detective achieves an AUPRC of 0.796 and a Recall of 0.847.
papers.authors: Maria-Ioana-Andrea Ivan, Orhan Ermis, Ruxandra F. Olimid

papers.title: BrowseSafe++: Benchmarking Prompt Injection Detection Across Web Contexts, Languages, and Browser Views
papers.abstract: Browser agents need to make decisions and execute actions on behalf of users while consuming untrusted webpages, creating opportunities for malicious instructions embedded in webpages to redirect legitimate tasks. We introduce BrowseSafe++, which extends BrowseSafe from 14,719 pages to 38,675 pairs of pages. Most of its prompt injections were observed in the wild on production websites. We keep each injection unchanged and rewrite the sensitive parts of the page around it to protect privacy. Each attacked page has a clean copy of the same page as its control. Both are provided as HTML, Markdown, an accessibility tree, and a screenshot. Every pair includes a user task and its expected answer. The benchmark includes twelve types of websites, from news articles to shared documents and forums, with 24 attack types appearing in 18 different locations on a page. We use these paired pages to train BrowseSafe-Guard, two 0.8B-parameter detectors for text and screenshots. Both achieve higher F1 scores than the detector based on frontier models, while keeping false-positive rates on benign pages and inference cost low. BrowseSafe-Adapt revises benchmark injections from browser-agent feedback, and attacks that succeed on only a few percent of tasks when replayed directly reach up to 95.41% success once adapted.
papers.authors: Yuetian Chen, Kaiyuan Zhang, Yuntao Du, Thomas Li, Mark Tenenholtz, Kyle Polley, Jerry Ma, Denis Yarats, Ninghui Li

papers.title: StableJudge: A Lightweight Adversarial Defense Framework for LLM-as-a-Judge
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to assign scalar scores that drive downstream decision-making, including tasks such as paper review and recommendation. However, LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines are vulnerable to score-hijacking prompt injection embedded in evaluated content, which corrupts scoring signals and distorts induced rankings. Existing defenses often enforce robustness by modifying the judge model itself, making safety dependent on a specific model's scale and training and requiring repeated effort when the judge is updated or replaced. We propose StableJudge, a lightweight defense framework that externalizes prompt-injection mitigation as a reusable pre-scoring capability. StableJudge centers on a compact 0.13B Sentry that localizes injected spans and performs targeted sanitization prior to evaluation, and is trained using adversarially evolving attacks to improve robustness beyond a fixed prompt set. To stabilize measurement, StableJudge derives deterministic, fine-grained scalar scores from the judge's output distribution. Across held-out scientific abstracts and out-of-distribution attack variants, StableJudge improves score recovery under attack while largely preserving general-purpose performance, demonstrating that robust LLM-based judging can be achieved by decoupling safety from judge scale via reusable defense capabilities. Code and data will be released.
papers.authors: Anning Hu, Yangyu Li, Yuqi Huang, Shengchao Hu, Junchi Yan

papers.title: When Does Trust Help? A Leakage-Free Evaluation of Representation- and Aggregation-Based Defenses Against Backdoors in Federated Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) lets distributed intrusion-detection systems (IDS) train on private traffic, but exposes the global model to poisoning and backdoor attacks under non-IID client data. A popular defense family scores or filters clients using a small trusted "root" dataset and the similarity of client behaviour to a trusted reference. I re-examine these trust-based defenses under a protocol designed to remove common evaluation artifacts: train-only feature standardization, a server root set disjoint from client data, multi-seed (n=6) runs with paired significance tests, formal (varepsilon, delta) accounting for DP-SGD, and a defense-aware adaptive attacker. Across three NIDS datasets (CSE-CIC-IDS2018, NF-ToN-IoT, NF-UNSW-NB15-v2) I find: (1) a representation-similarity aggregator (RepGuard) significantly improves classification utility and seed-stability over FLTrust under heavy non-IID poisoning, and - under severe heterogeneity or many adversaries - also lowers backdoor ASR substantially (e.g., 0.48 vs FLTrust 0.86 at Dirichlet alpha=0.1); (2) at strong trigger magnitudes no defense reduces backdoor attack success rate (ASR approx 0.95); (3) a controlled trigger-magnitude sweep shows defenses help only for small triggers (ASR 0.10 for RepGuard at magnitude 0.5, vs. 0.40 undefended) and collapse to ASR approx 1.0 by magnitude 2; (4) a triggered-canary check that assumes knowledge of the attacker's trigger - the assumption behind much prior "success" - lowers ASR from 0.49 to 0.12, i.e., trigger knowledge, not representation scoring, suppresses the backdoor; (5) correctly-accounted DP-SGD (varepsilon in [0.3, 16]) costs little utility but does not mitigate the backdoor. I release the protocol so future FL-IDS defenses can be evaluated without the leakage and oracle assumptions that inflate reported robustness.
papers.authors: Shiddarth Dey Tusar, Zawad Yalmie Sazid

papers.title: TRAP: Tree-Guided Reinforcement-Augmented Probing for Automated LLM Jailbreaking
papers.abstract: Aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that circumvent their safety guardrails, making the identification of these vulnerabilities important for understanding and mitigating model weaknesses. Existing automated jailbreak methods explore prompt candidates or reuse attack experience, but generally do not learn over a persistent hierarchy that connects related jailbreak strategies, such as role-play, encoding, and obfuscation. This leaves the relationships among reusable strategies underused in guiding adaptive attack selection. We present Tree-Guided Reinforcement-Augmented Probing (TRAP), a hierarchical framework for automated jailbreak strategy discovery that requires only black-box access to the target LLM. TRAP organizes established jailbreak methods and successful attack templates into a semantic strategy tree, connecting broad attack approaches to concrete, reusable strategies. A reinforcement-learning policy based on a tree-structured gradient bandit explores this tree and uses evaluator feedback to update strategy preferences along each selected path. The policy retains these preferences across attack objectives, allowing experience from earlier attempts to guide subsequent strategy selection. Retrieval-augmented prompt construction translates the selected strategy into an attack for the current objective using relevant successful examples. Experiments on AdvBench across seven aligned LLMs show that TRAP outperforms its counterparts on six models under the reported method settings and the common primary evaluator, achieving attack success rates of 45.6% to 97.9% on these models. These findings support hierarchical strategy learning as an effective approach to discovering jailbreak vulnerabilities in aligned LLMs.
papers.authors: Mohammad Reza Mirbagheri, Amir Mahdi Sadeghzadeh

papers.title: Toward Realistic Privacy Risk in FL-Enabled OT Intrusion Detection Systems
papers.abstract: In Operational Technology (OT) environments, Federated Learning (FL) is increasingly adopted to train Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) without sharing raw operational data across facilities. However, model updates may still leak sensitive information about industrial processes, creating privacy risks that remain largely invisible within current OT security architectures. Existing reference models, including the Purdue hierarchy, do not explicitly represent the FL learning lifecycle, making privacy leakage difficult to observe and evaluate. To address this gap, we introduce the ML Plane, a novel architectural abstraction that integrates FL workflows within OT systems, enabling visibility of learning-related information flows that are not explicitly represented in traditional OT architectures. Building on the proposed ML Plane, we outline a privacy auditing framework for FL-enabled OT systems. The framework uses Federated Membership Inference Attacks (FedMIA) as an initial assessment mechanism and is being instantiated within a Smart Grid testbed to support the future evaluation of privacy risks under realistic OT deployment constraints.
papers.authors: Assunta Imperatrice, Luigi ROmano

papers.title: CT0: Cybersecurity Transformer
papers.abstract: General-purpose frontier models are large, expensive to run, and increasingly reluctant to engage with authorised defensive- and offensive-security work. We ask the opposite question: how small can a cybersecurity-specialist transformer be while remaining genuinely useful to a security practitioner? We introduce CT0, a Cybersecurity Transformer architecture, and CT0-Micro, its first incarnation: a compact (~4B-parameter) model built on the open base model, whose backbone is specialised by two-phase on-policy distillation on our Cybersecurity AI (CAI) dataset. CT0 serves two modes from one set of weights: System 1 answers typed security decisions (is this file suspicious, is this request an attack, did the model just refuse) in a single forward pass without generating a token, System 2 is the usual tool-using agent, and a confidence gate spends generation only where the fast path is unsure. Specialisation lifts the agentic path: CT0-Micro solves 21.1% of cybench-subtask against 7.6% for its base, above every open model of comparable footprint and the densest cybersecurity capability per parameter we measured. The fast path is what the architecture buys: CT0-Micro screens eighty files per second for indicators of compromise, catches its own refusals at 96.5% accuracy in 47 ms where the model judging itself reaches 76.5% in 254 ms and misses half of them, flags jailbreak requests at AUROC 0.966 in 8 ms, and, generating only for the facts it is unsure about, extracts vulnerability facts more accurately than either mode alone at a fifth of the generative cost. All of it is built in about 314 RTX PRO 6000 GPU-hours and served from one workstation GPU, with no policy layer between operator and target. Across eighteen benchmarks and use cases run with one checkpoint and head, we report where the design helps, where it does not, and what it still lacks.
papers.authors: Víctor Mayoral-Vilches

papers.title: ATTCK-R: Knowledge-Aware Long-Horizon Jailbreaking for Protected LLMs
papers.abstract: As large language models are deployed behind increasingly sophisticated safety mechanisms, evaluating their robustness under realistic adversarial conditions becomes increasingly difficult and critical. Existing jailbreaking evaluations often rely on static prompts, limited interaction horizons, or lightly protected systems, failing to reflect protected deployment settings with prompt-based safety protections. We show that the introduction of a prompt-based safety protection reduces the average attack success rate of a strong multi-turn baseline from 0.896 to 0.608 (32.1\% relative), demonstrating that unprotected evaluations substantially overestimate real-world vulnerabilities. We propose Adaptive Traceback and Tactic Curation for Knowledge-based Red-teaming (ATTCK-R), a planning-driven multi-turn red teaming framework designed for protected black-box systems. ATTCK-R models jailbreaking as a long-horizon trajectory optimization problem using a structured belief state, introduces optimization-based tactic curation to abstract reusable strategies from prior successes and failures, and employs informed traceback to resume attacks from strategically meaningful states rather than restarting. Evaluated across 9 widely used LLMs configured with a single prompt-based safety protection layer, ATTCK-R consistently outperforms strong recent multi-turn jailbreaking frameworks. Ablation results confirm that long-horizon planning and tactic curation improve attack effectiveness, while adaptive traceback improves efficiency through structured recovery from conversational failure.
papers.authors: Md Mushfiqur Rahman, Tobias Rohde, Rahul Tripathi, Khalil Elkhalil, Kevin Lybarger

papers.title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking
papers.authors: Lass Najmuldeen, Seyedhamidreza Mousavi

papers.title: Witness-Succinct UC-Secure SNARKs with Weaker Trust Assumptions
papers.abstract: Zero-knowledge Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments of Knowledge (zkSNARKs) are foundational cryptographic primitives enabling privacy-preserving and verifiable computation. However, most existing zkSNARK constructions rely on strong trust assumptions—typically a fully trusted setup—which undermines their applicability in adversarial or decentralized environments. Although transparent zkSNARKs remove this assumption, they typically do not satisfy strong composability guarantees such as Universal Composability (UC). In this work, we present the first framework for constructing UC-secure zkSNARKs under weaker trust assumptions, based on a new primitive called Key-Updatable Polynomial Commitments (KU-pCom). This primitive enables publicly verifiable commitment-key updates, requiring only one honest update rather than a fully trusted setup. Our compiler transforms any Simulation-Extractable zkSNARK into a UC-secure variant by composing it with a KU-pCom scheme. We instantiate our framework in two settings: (1) using the structured, trusted setup of the KZG commitment scheme, and (2) an instantiation based on the lattice-based commitment scheme of Hwang et al. (Crypto 2024). We implement both instantiations and provide an end-to-end benchmark of UC-secure zkSNARKs with succinctness. Compared to prior UC-secure NIZKs that sacrifice succinctness (e.g., Abdolmaleki et al., CSF 2024), our work demonstrates that UC security, succinctness, and practical efficiency can be simultaneously achieved, establishing a new foundation for succinct, composable proof systems under weaker trust assumptions.
papers.authors: Nahid Roustaeifar, Maryam Zarezadeh, Neel Mehendale, Behzad Abdolmaleki, Mahshid Delavar, Stefan Köpsell

papers.title: Lattice Bingo: Asynchrony and One-Shot Adaptivity in Verifiable Secret Sharing via Erasure Code Commitments
papers.abstract: Asynchronous verifiable secret sharing (AVSS) allows a dealer to distribute a secret among parties while preserving privacy and consistent reconstruction, despite Byzantine faults and arbitrary message delays. It is a fundamental building block for Byzantine agreement, distributed key generation, and secure multiparty computation. Packed AVSS protocols share many secrets together to reduce communication per secret. The best known AVSS protocols achieve quadratic communication while sharing linearly many secrets. In particular, Bingo (Abraham et al., CRYPTO 2023) shares a batch of $\Theta(k)$ secrets among $k$ parties using $O(\lambda k^2)$ words of communication, while also achieving adaptive security, but relies on assumptions that are not post-quantum secure. Known post-quantum alternatives have higher worst-case communication for comparable batch sizes or require substantially larger batches to achieve linear amortized communication. We present Lattice Bingo, a lattice-based packed AVSS protocol with quadratic communication and linear packing. For every constant $\epsilon>0$, it shares $\Theta(k)$ secrets among $k\geq(3+\epsilon)f$ parties, tolerates $f$ Byzantine parties, and uses $O(k^2\operatorname{poly}(\lambda))$ words of communication. It additionally achieves one-shot adaptive secrecy: the adversary may adaptively choose its corruption and reconstruction requests based on the public transcript observed so far, but must submit these requests together in a single batch. Our main technical contribution is a commitment scheme for two-dimensional linear codes based on the PowerBASIS assumption. We combine PowerBASIS commitments with the linear code based secret sharing of Applebaum, Nir, and Pinkas, replacing the Reed–Solomon encoding and KZG commitments used in Bingo. Our commitment supports proof interpolation, enabling parties to recover missing shares and their opening proofs. It additionally achieves a notion that we call one-shot simulation hiding. Together, these properties allow us to adapt Bingo’s framework to obtain Lattice Bingo with the same efficiency and one-shot adaptive security.
papers.authors: Ittai Abraham, Aniket Kate, Aditi Partap, Ertem Nusret Tas

papers.title: Sample-Preserving Search-to-Decision Reduction for Noisy Linear Equations over Large Moduli
papers.abstract: The Noisy Linear Equations problem involves finding the solution to a random linear system over a finite field given noisy evaluations. This is a generalisation of various learning problems widely used in cryptography, including Learning with Errors (LWE), Learning with Rounding (LWR), and Learning Parity with Noise (LPN). We present a new sample-preserving search-to-decision reduction for Noisy Linear Equations that has complexity $\mathrm{poly}(n,m,\log q, q/σ)$, where $n$ is the dimension of the secret, $m$ is the number of samples, $q$ is the modulus, and $σ$ is the magnitude of the noise (defined suitably for the kind of noise involved). In particular, this implies search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR that run in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ even if the modulus $q$ is exponentially large, as long as the noise-to-modulus ratio $σ/q$ is non-negligible. Our reduction works for prime moduli $q$. If $q$ is composite, it instead produces a list that contains a small multiple of the solution. Prior to this work, known search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR either did not preserve the parameters of the problem (i.e., $m$, $n$, $σ$, and $q$), or had complexity that scaled polynomially with either $σ$ or the largest prime factor of $q$.
papers.authors: Andrej Bogdanov, Kel Zin Tan, Prashant Nalini Vasudevan

papers.title: Sample-Preserving Search-to-Decision Reduction for Noisy Linear Equations over Large Moduli

papers.authors: Andrej Bogdanov, Kel Zin Tan, Prashant Nalini Vasudevan

papers.title: Mercury: Fuzzy Private Set Intersection with Communication and Computation Logarithmic in the Threshold
papers.abstract: Private Set Intersection (PSI) allows two mutually distrusting parties to compute the intersection of their sets without revealing any additional information and has found numerous applications. The approximate matching required by various applications has led to the development of Fuzzy PSI (FPSI), a variant of PSI that identifies approximate intersection elements under a public distance threshold \(\delta\). Reducing computation and communication costs remains an important challenge for FPSI. In this paper, we present a new FPSI protocol, called Mercury, which achieves logarithmic computation and communication complexity with respect to threshold \(\delta\). Our protocol exploits the correlation of the intersection and the point pairs held by the parties, and efficiently identifies the neighboring point pairs by a mixed protocol from homomorphic encryption and secure two-party computation using a "mask-then-compare" technique. We implemented Mercury and evaluated both its sender-private and standard FPSI variants. For balanced two-dimensional inputs, Mercury-SP achieves \(9.0\sim63.9\times\) runtime speedups and reduces communication by a factor of \(8.7\sim26.1\) across the evaluated thresholds and set sizes in the LAN setting, compared to the FPSI protocol by Dang et al. (CCS'25). In the completed unbalanced experiments, Mercury-SP achieves \(55.7\sim132.4\times\) WAN runtime speedups compared to the FPSI protocol by Piske et al. (CCS'25).
papers.authors: Qi Liu, Kang Yang, Binwu Xiang, Xiaojie Guo, Cheng Hong, Yu Yu

papers.title: Succinct Arguments with (almost) Minimal Time and Space Overheads from Symmetric-Key Primitives
papers.abstract: We construct public-coin, succinct, zero-knowledge interactive arguments for NP relations decided by time-$T$, space-$S$ random-access machines. Assuming the existence of collision-resistant hash functions, our arguments give a frontier of tradeoffs between prover time and space, and proof size. We follow the streaming PIOP+PCS framework of Block et al. (TCC 2020, CRYPTO 2021), reducing the problem of constructing time- and space-efficient arguments to time- and space-efficient streaming multilinear polynomial commitment schemes (MLPCS). We develop two code-based streaming MLPCS inspired by Brakedown (CRYPTO 2023) and BaseFold (CRYPTO 2024), implementing each scheme when additionally given succinct access to the underlying encoding matrices. We instantiate this framework assuming row-sparse, column-sparse, and Reed-Solomon encoders, then apply a generic PIOP + MLPCS compiler to obtain our (zero-knowledge) time- and space-efficient arguments. Finally, as all our protocols are public-coin, applying Fiat-Shamir yields time- and space-efficient (zk)SNARKs from symmetric-key primitives (i.e., collision-resistant hashing). Our Brakedown-based constructions have \(O(\log T)\) rounds and \(\widetilde O(\sqrt T)\)-size proofs and verification time, with two complementary prover profiles: (i) \(\widetilde O(S)\) space (which is optimal) and \(\widetilde O(T^{3/2})\) time, and (ii) \(\widetilde O(T)\) time (nearly optimal) and \(\widetilde O(S+\sqrt T)\) space. Our BaseFold-based constructions achieve $\mathrm{polylog}(T)$ proof size and verification time with \(O(\log T)\) rounds. We again obtain two complementary prover profiles: (i) an encoder parameterized construction with \(\widetilde O(T+T_{\mathrm{Enc}})\) time and \(\widetilde O(S + S_{\mathrm{Enc}})\) space, where \(T_{\mathrm{Enc}}, S_{\mathrm{Enc}}\) are the running time and space of a streaming log-space encoder for a suitable linear code, and (ii) an unconditional sub-quadratic instantiation \(\widetilde O(T^{3/2})\) time and \(\widetilde O(S+\sqrt T)\) space.
papers.authors: Alexander R. Block, Caleb Geren, Pratik Soni

papers.title: Secrets in Preamble: Practical and Robust PHY Information Hiding for Wi-Fi
papers.abstract: Physical layer (PHY) information hiding refers to the concealment of secrets within PHY waveforms without compromising the integrity of the primary communication link, thereby enabling critical applications such as covert communication, PHY steganography, and watermarking. The widespread deployment of Wi-Fi has motivated substantial research interest in hiding secrets within Wi-Fi waveforms. However, existing Wi-Fi information hiding approaches suffer from two limitations: restricted steganographic capacity and insufficient robustness against environmental variations, both of which severely constrain practical deployment. This work proposes to embed secrets within the Wi-Fi legacy short training field (L-STF). The designed method preserves the autocorrelation properties of Wi-Fi L-STF, ensuring that packet detection and coarse frequency offset compensation functionalities remain uncompromised. The secret embedding and extraction processes employ a pair of neural networks designed to learn optimal embedding rules and maximize steganographic capacity. We developed a prototype system and conducted comprehensive experiments across both indoor and outdoor environments. Experimental results show that our method can reliably embed 46 secret bits within Wi-Fi packets across diverse channel conditions, achieving significantly enhanced steganographic capacity and environmental robustness. The hardware prototype study validates the feasibility of the proposed Wi-Fi information hiding scheme.
papers.authors: Rui Pan, Guanxiong Shen, Linning Peng, Xinyu Qi, Junqing Zhang

papers.title: Magnetar: High-speed post-quantum RV64 zkVM from standard hashes
papers.abstract: We describe the design, implementation, and experimental evaluation of Magnetar, a transparent proof system for RV64I program executions (i.e., a zkVM). Magnetar is the first zkVM to simultaneously satisfy the following three properties: 1. General-purpose proving. Magnetar proves programs compiled to the general-purpose RV64I ISA. An implementation of the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) written in Rust or Go can therefore run inside Magnetar, yielding a zkEVM for proving executions of existing EVM smart contracts. 2. Hash-based, post-quantum security. Magnetar’s cryptographic security is rooted in standard hash functions (e.g., SHA-256 or SHA-3). 3. Efficient recursion. Magnetar’s verification work is dominated by evaluating standard hash functions. Magnetar’s proof engine, BinarySpartan, is well-suited for such bit-oriented computations, so verifying a proof is itself an efficient proving workload. Unlike prior general-purpose zkVMs, Magnetar does not rely on circuit-friendly algebraic hash functions such as Poseidon or Poseidon2, elliptic-curve or lattice assumptions, or a conjectured Reed–Solomon proximity gap. Even prior zkVMs commonly described as hash-based rely on elliptic-curve or lattice assumptions in their core proving machinery, provide only about 100 bits of security, or rest on conjectured soundness; some do more than one of these. Finally, we implement Magnetar in Rust and experimentally evaluate it. We find that, at 120 bits of provable security and with 12 performance cores on an M4 Max MacBook Pro, Magnetar proves 2^{22}-cycle executions at 7.2–8.7 million cycles per second, with proofs of about 600 KiB that verify in 11–13 ms. Across 15 application workloads, Magnetar’s proving throughput is 24–66× that of SP1 Hypercube, a hash-and-more-based zkVM; 12–37× that of Jolt-Dory, a curve-based zkVM; and 6–20× that of Jolt-Akita, a lattice-based zkVM, with geometric-mean speedups of about 39×, 18×, and 9.6×, respectively. An optimized Magnetar proves 222-cycle executions at 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each geometric-mean speedup by about 1.3×. Magnetar’s proofs are about 4.6× smaller than SP1 Hypercube’s; Jolt’s proofs are under 100 KiB, but they rely on elliptic-curve or lattice assumptions.
papers.authors: Srinath Setty

papers.title: Individual Cryptography from Iterated Squaring
papers.abstract: Individual cryptography (Dziembowski et al. Crypto'23) and complete knowledge (Kelkar et al. CCS'24) aim at constructing protocols that ensure that some individual party must know a secret value in the clear, and so the computation cannot have been “outsourced” to an MPC computation. Two central primitives are proofs of complete (or individual) knowledge, which enforce that some party actually knows the secret witness, and secret sharing with snitching, which enforces that whenever the secret is reconstructed, some party must learn a certificate of this fact. The instantiations proposed by both papers (Crypto'23 and CCS'24) ensure that to compute a proof or reconstruct the shared secret, a large number of hash function evaluations is necessary. Thus, at least one party must compute many of these “in the clear” (and not via MPC) and from the hash function inputs one can extract the secret (in the random oracle model). In practice, they suggest using Bitcoin mining hardware. Sequential proofs of complete knowledge have recently been proposed, which use proofs of sequential work to enforce that the hashes are performed sequentially. As a consequence, it suffices to require a much smaller number of hashes, and thus such primitives can be implemented on standard hardware. Unfortunately, this approach does not work for primitives like secret sharing, as one would need to efficiently sample the challenge for the sequential computation together with its solution. In this work, we leverage ideas from time-lock puzzles to overcome this issue. We construct secret sharing with snitching and encryption with self-incriminating proofs where reconstruction/decryption is sequential. The security of our scheme relies on a new knowledge assumption, which informally states that whenever parties that hold secret shares of an RSA modulus N=pq jointly compute 2^2^T N for some large T (too large to perform a sequential computation of length T in MPC), then at least one of them must have learned a multiple of N.
papers.authors: Georg Fuchsbauer, Christoph U. Günther, Charlotte Hoffmann, Krzysztof Pietrzak, Fabian Regen

papers.title: Barely Sublinear RAM-FHE from Plain LWE
papers.abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption for RAM programs (RAM-FHE), introduced by Hamlin, Holmgren, Weiss, and Wichs (Crypto 2019), allows a server to evaluate a RAM program on encrypted data at a per-step cost sublinear in the memory size $N$, whereas standard FHE must read the entire memory for every memory access. In a celebrated work, Lin, Mook, and Wichs (STOC 2023) gave the first, and to date the only, construction from a concrete assumption, namely Ring-LWE. In this work, we construct a RAM-FHE scheme from plain LWE that evaluates each step of a RAM program in $o(N/\log N)$ time. While the scheme is barely sublinear, even such a slight saving over the linear cost of standard FHE was not known to be achievable from unstructured, plain LWE. As Lin, Mook, and Wichs did, we build RAM-FHE by extending a Doubly-Efficient Private Information Retrieval (DEPIR) scheme. Since the only DEPIR from plain LWE, due to Lee (Crypto 2026), relies on a Common Reference String (CRS) that is incompatible with the extension, we show how to remove the CRS and obtain a DEPIR from plain LWE in the standard model, which may be of independent interest.
papers.authors: Keewoo Lee

papers.title: Provably Subexponential Algorithms for Bounded-Error LWE with Few Samples
papers.abstract: We show that a variant of the Wagner/BKW-style algorithm for LWE of Kirchner and Fouque [KF15] solves decision and search LWE with secrets of size $n$ over prime moduli $q=n^{κ+o(1)}$, for any fixed $κ>0$, with errors bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, in time $2^{O(n/\ln\ln n)}$ given $n+O(n/\ln\ln n)$ original samples. Further, if each coordinate of the secret is also bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, the same time bound holds with errors bounded by $n^{o(1)}$ and only $O(n/\ln\ln q)$ samples. Earlier, it was known that Kirchner and Fouque's algorithm could solve LWE with these parameters in subexponential time with a much larger number of samples $m = Ω(n\log{n})$ [HKM18]. Ducas et al. [DEL25] showed that an adaptation of this algorithm could solve the corresponding dual, the $\mathrm{SIS}^{\infty}$ problem, with a suitable norm bound $q/\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ and $m=n+ω(n/\ln\ln n)$ variables in subexponential time. Whereas their analysis involves interpreting the algorithm in terms of chains of lattices, our approach is quite elementary and is based on bounding the lower moments of a Fourier statistic.
papers.authors: Haoxing Lin, Prashant Nalini Vasudevan

papers.title: Provably Subexponential Algorithms for Bounded-Error LWE with Few Samples
papers.abstract: We show that a variant of the Wagner/BKW-style algorithm for LWE of Kirchner and Fouque [KF15] solves decision and search LWE with secrets of size $n$ over prime moduli $q=n^{\kappa+o(1)}$, for any fixed $\kappa>0$, with errors bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, in time $2^{O(n/\ln\ln n)}$ given $n+O(n/\ln\ln n)$ original samples. Ducas et al. Whereas their analysis involves interpreting the algorithm in terms of chains of lattices, our approach is quite elementary and is based on bounding the lower moments of a Fourier statistic.
papers.authors: Haoxing Lin, Prashant Nalini Vasudevan

papers.title: Verifiable Computation on Encrypted Data from Homomorphic Encryption over Random Encodings
papers.abstract: Verifiable Computation on Encrypted Data (vCOED) enables clients to outsource computation while providing both privacy and integrity. A promising vCOED paradigm is blind proofs, which use homomorphic encryption (HE) to evaluate verifiable computation (VC) proofs on encrypted data. Despite their efficiency, blind proofs do not provide strong client privacy: a malicious server can exploit reaction attacks to learn information about the client's inputs, intermediate values or final outputs. Our work addresses this limitation by introducing Homomorphic Encryption over Random Encodings (HERE). We formalize a new security notion, indistinguishability under chosen-plaintext attacks in the presence of an equality oracle over encodings (IND-CPA-E). We prove that combining IND-CPA-E-secure HERE schemes with blind proofs that verify computation over the encodings yields vCOED protocols with strong client privacy. We then instantiate a HERE scheme for functions of bounded degree $d$, using Shamir secret sharing at $(d+1)$ evaluation points under $(d+1)$ distinct HE keys. Finally, we demonstrate the concrete efficiency of our approach through an application to matrix-vector multiplication (MVM), a linear computation corresponding to $d=1$. The proof overhead (i.e. the ratio of the vCOED prover runtime to the homomorphic MVM runtime) in our combined vCOED protocol is as low as $2\times$, as demonstrated in our prototype implementation.
papers.authors: Jiayi Kang, Erik Pohle, Jannik Spiessens

papers.title: Efficient Unbiasable Verifiable Random Functions via (Non-)Black-Box Reductions
papers.abstract: We present conceptually simple and practically efficient constructions of a verifiable random function (VRF) that fulfills strong notions of unbiasability recently introduced by Giunta and Stewart (Eurocrypt 2024). Unbiasability is a crucial property for many applications of VRFs such as leader election in proof-of-stake blockchains. The only previous constructions provide heuristic security in the random oracle model or rely on the decisional Diffie–Hellman assumption with preprocessing which incurs significant overhead. In contrast, our compiler turns any VRF into an unbiasable VRF in the standard model (without any setup) using only symmetric-key primitives; and thus only with negligible computational overhead. Underlying our approach, we provide a generic black-box reduction for unbiasability of VRFs that incurs subexponential loss. Additionally, under a mild (verifiable) requirement on the underlying VRF we also show a novel non-black-box reduction that incurs only polynomial loss. This non-black-box technique allows us to replace the folklore "VUF-then-Hash" heuristic with a provably secure "Hash-then-VRF" construction at virtually no cost. In particular, if the underlying VRF hashes its input, our transformation requires only a single evaluation of a hardcore function, e.g. parity of the input (plus a PRF evaluation for full security).
papers.authors: Nicholas Brandt

papers.title: Average-Case Hardness of Lattice Problems in Special Genera of Fixed Rank
papers.abstract: The distinguishing variant $\Delta$LIP of the Lattice Isomorphism Problem underlies the security proofs of a growing family of lattice-based schemes. As the special genus is the strongest efficiently computable invariant of a lattice, such a proof may replace the lattice used by the scheme with a random lattice of the same genus. This raises the question of how hard lattice problems actually are on such random lattices. We answer it, under GRH, with a worst-case to average-case reduction inside any special genus $\mathcal{G}$ of Hermitian lattices of fixed rank $r \geq 2$ over a cyclotomic field $K$ of degree $d$: for each of $\mathrm{(H)SVP}$, $\mathrm{HCVP}$, $(\Delta)\mathrm{BDD}$, $\mathrm{DSP}$ and $\mathrm{DGS}$, solving the problem on a random class of $\mathcal{G}$, drawn from its natural distribution, is as hard as solving it on the worst-case lattice of $\mathcal{G}$, at the cost of a factor $p = \mathrm{poly}(d) \cdot {\det}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\Lambda)^{O_r(1)/d}$ in the approximation factor. The reduction is a random walk on the Kneser $\mathfrak{p}$-neighbour graph of $\mathcal{G}$: neighbours stay close enough to transfer problem instances, while the walk equidistributes quickly, a fact we deduce from spectral bounds for the associated Hecke operators. As an application we give a direct and tight security proof for a minimal LIP-based KEM, resting on two independent assumptions: that the lattice it uses is indistinguishable from a random lattice of its genus, and that $\Delta$BDD is hard on that genus. Unlike existing LIP-based proofs, this requires neither an ad-hoc lattice of the form $q\Lambda \oplus (q+1)\Lambda$, nor the tightness loss caused by the dense sublattice such proofs rely on.
papers.authors: Koen de Boer, Maxime Bombar, Aurel Page, Wessel van Woerden

papers.title: Fast Polynomial Arithmetic in the Exponent without Roots of Unity
papers.abstract: In cryptographic algorithms based on groups in which the discrete logarithm is supposed to be hard, it is frequent to perform polynomial arithmetic in the exponent of group elements. This old technique has become a critical operation in many recent advanced protocols, mostly related to commitments and zero-knowledge proofs, where polynomials of high degrees are involved. Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) techniques in the exponent are often implemented to gain speed. However, they require roots of unity to exist in the field GF(q) where q is the order of the group. In this work, we propose algorithms that preserve the quasi-linear complexity of the Fourier Transforms, even when no root of unity are available. For this, we develop a formalism for the algebraic structure of polynomials with coefficients in a group, that allows us to adapt asymptotically fast polynomial multiplication algorithms to the case of arithmetic in the exponent. In particular, we design an algorithm inspired by the Schönhage-Strassen algorithm, which runs about twice slower than NTT but does not require any arithmetic property on the order of the group. We explain how this can be adapted to batched KZG commitment proofs and the Bayer-Groth verifiable mixnet used in e-voting.
papers.authors: Diane Ducrocq, Pierrick Gaudry

papers.title: Separating One-Way Functions from Verifiable Delay Functions
papers.abstract: Timed cryptography captures computations that inherently require a prescribed amount of time, even in the presence of parallelism, and has emerged as a central notion due to its broad applications in both practice and theory. A natural question is how timed cryptographic primitives relate to traditional cryptography, in particular to primitives in Minicrypt. Guan and Montgomery (CRYPTO 2024) show that sequential functions do not imply one-way functions (OWFs) via black-box reductions. Their result, however, leaves open whether adding public verifiability (a substantially stronger requirement) suffices to imply OWFs. We study this question via verifiable delay functions (VDFs), which require substantial sequential time to evaluate, yet produce a unique output that is efficiently and publicly verifiable. We show that VDFs do not imply OWFs via fully black-box, relativizing reductions. Combined with prior results showing that VDFs cannot be constructed in the random oracle model, this establishes that there is no black-box implication in either direction between VDFs and OWFs. Our proof develops a new oracle separation technique that combines the random oracle with a carefully designed complexity-theoretic oracle inspired by Kolmogorov complexity.
papers.authors: Hamza Abusalah, Nicholas Brandt, Ziyi Guan, Kristina Hostáková

papers.title: ECGWmark: Deep Watermarking for Electrocardiogram Signals
papers.abstract: Secure transmission of electrocardiogram (ECG) signals remains a major challenge in telecardiology. While traditional mathematical watermarking can embed patient metadata directly into ECG signals, it is highly fragile against temporal desynchronization such as circular phase shifts. In contrast, existing deep watermarking approaches for temporal signals, such as audio, typically rely on lossy quantization, which compromises the high-frequency micro-morphological details critical for clinical diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we propose ECGWmark, a fully convolutional and quantization-free deep watermarking framework for medical time-series. ECGWmark operates in a continuous, full-resolution latent space and utilizes a localized frame-level mechanism to improve the robustness to severe desynchronization. Crucially, we introduce a differentiable Physiological Loss guided by a clinical classifier to preserve diagnostic semantics. Experiments on the benchmark MIT-BIH database show that ECGWmark maintains channel-bit extraction accuracy above 90% under the evaluated circular temporal shifts. Furthermore, under a rigorous inter-patient diagnostic evaluation, Class-V sensitivity changes from 71.97% to 76.50%, whereas Macro-F1 changes from 35.25% to 34.71% and Class-S sensitivity from 8.89% to 1.39%; these results indicate mixed class-level effects.
papers.authors: Kuan-Yu Chen, Kuan-Chen Wang, Yu Tsao, Jian-Jiun Ding

papers.title: Post-Quantum Session Establishment for Matter over Thread: Message Size, Transport, and Protocol Options
papers.abstract: Matter's first post-quantum change protects device attestation with ML-DSA, but its operational handshake, CASE, still derives session keys from P-256 ECDH, so recorded traffic can be decrypted once a quantum computer exists. We quantify the cost of moving CASE to ML-KEM and post-quantum signatures over Thread, where frames carry at most 127 bytes and a Matter message at most 1178 bytes. A byte-exact model of the CASE messages shows that a drop-in ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-44 handshake grows from 1.6 kB to 22.8 kB and that no fully post-quantum configuration built from FIPS 203/204/205 algorithms fits the message limit. A Monte Carlo model of multi-hop Thread, calibrated to OpenThread and Matter source constants, shows that sending these messages as fragmented IPv6 datagrams causes spurious retransmissions whenever a message and its reply outlast Matter's retransmission timer. At three to four hops the drop-in handshake then takes 1.8 to 2.6 times longer than with a selective-repeat block transfer, with or without interference, and up to 33% of handshakes with sleepy devices fail; raising the timers does not remove the effect. Caching certificate chains and authenticating the device with a pre-distributed ML-KEM key reduce the handshake to 6.1 kB and 44 ms of device computation. As a first step, hybrid P-256+ML-KEM-512 key exchange with a cached device chain protects session keys against harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks while every message still fits the current limit.
papers.authors: Daniel Commey

papers.title: Provable Subexponential Algorithms for Module-SIS and Module-LWE
papers.abstract: Ducas, Engelberts and Loyer (CRYPTO 2025) turned Wagner's generalized birthday algorithm into a provable subexponential-time Gaussian sampler for unstructured short integer solutions. Recent preprints of Han, Gao and Hu, and of Chen, Jiang, Wang and Zhang, obtain low-sample decision learning-with-errors algorithms from this framework. We extend it to module matrices over power-of-two cyclotomic rings, for every residue degree of the prime modulus. For fixed module ranks $k,\ell\ge1$, let $n=kd$, $m=(k+\ell)d$, and suppose $\ln(q/\sqrt n)=(\ln n)^{b+o(1)}$. For every fixed $b,c,\xi>0$, we solve Module-SIS with coefficient infinity-norm bound $q/(\ln n)^c$ in worst-case time and space $2^{(1/(2b)+\xi)n/\ln\ln n}$. For matrix-independent errors satisfying $\|e\|\le\sigma\sqrt m$ with probability $1-o(1)$ and $\ln(2+\sigma)=(\ln n)^{a+o(1)}$, $0\le a 1/2$, one ring sample and growing rank suffice for decision and search in time and space $2^{(1/2+\xi)n/\ln\ln n}$ when the sample supplies $(1+o(1))n/\ln\ln n$ scalar responses. Here ``narrow'' restricts both secret and error. Separate heuristic estimates in the model of Ducas, Engelberts and Loyer suggest that Wagner-style attacks do not reach the NIST security targets of ML-KEM and ML-DSA.
papers.authors: William Youmans

papers.title: Optimal Statistical Oblivious RAM and Search Tree in the External-Memory Model
papers.abstract: Oblivious RAM (ORAM) allows a trusted client to access (encrypted) data stored in untrusted memory, such that the access patterns reveal nothing about the data or the queries. It is well-known that any ORAM scheme must suffer from a logarithmic overhead. More precisely stated, each request must incur $\Omega(\log_B N)$ block transfers on average, where $N$ is the size of the logical memory and $B$ is the block size of the oblivious implementation. Moreover, the same lower bound extends to oblivious Search Trees (ST). For upper bounds, however, we have been long stuck with a $(\log_B N)^2$ curse on two fronts: (1) Log-squared curse for statistically secure ORAMs: although optimality is known for computationally secure ORAMs for $B = \Theta(1)$ or $B \geq \log^{1+\epsilon} N$ (where $\epsilon > 0$ is an arbitrarily small constant), progress has been stagnant when it comes to statistical security. (2) Log-squared curse for oblivious search trees: for search trees, we do not know how to overcome the log-squared curse even when allowing computational assumptions. In this paper, we break this long-standing log-squared curse for both oblivious search trees and statistically secure ORAM on broad parameter regimes: (1) Our first result gives an optimal, statistically secure ORAM with $O(\log_B N)$ cost as long as $B \geq \log^{1+\epsilon} N$. (2) Our second result gives an optimal, statistically secure oblivious search tree with $O(\log_B N)$ cost when $B \geq \log^{2+\epsilon} N$, matching the performance of the best known non-oblivious search trees in this parameter region. Notably, this means that for search trees, we can get obliviousness for free! The assumptions on $B$ required to achieve optimality are standard and mild. They not only coincide with the standard wide cache-line assumption prevalent in the classical algorithms literature, but also align well with the hardware-enclave architectures that employ oblivious algorithms in practice, such as the implementations of Signal and Meta.
papers.authors: Andrew Krapivin, Elaine Shi

papers.title: Distinguishers for the Squeezing of the Alternating Sponge and Duet
papers.abstract: Recently, the Institute of Commercial Cryptography Standards (ICCS) launched the Next Generation Commercial Cryptographic Algorithm Program (NGCC), which includes a standardization process for cryptographic hash functions. In this note, we analyze the mode of operation of Duet, one of the hash-function candidates. Duet is a permutation-based hash function directly inspired by the Alternating Sponge (ASP). Both constructions use two permutations on $b=r+c$ bits, split into an outer part of $r$ bits and an inner part of $c$ bits. We first present a distinguisher against ASP requiring $\mathcal{O}(2^r)$ permutation queries, which contradicts the claimed indifferentiability bound in a non-trivial parameter regime. We then introduce a distinguisher and a state-recovery attack against Duet. Both attacks require only a constant number of $h$-bit output blocks, with $h\leq c$, and $\mathcal{O}(2^{r+c-h})$ permutation queries. These attacks do not affect the claimed collision or preimage resistance, but they distinguish Duet's multi-block output from random, with consequences if Duet is used as a XOF or a KDF; state recovery also enables length extension.
papers.authors: Gaëtan Leurent, César Mathéus

papers.title: Rapid mixing in superspecial isogeny graphs
papers.abstract: We prove expansion properties of superspecial isogeny graphs in dimension $g \geq 2$, including arbitrary level structure. In particular, we provide explicit bounds for the spectral gap, and a fine characterization of obstructions created by level structures (disconnectedness and periodicity). Without the level structure (the only case which was previously studied), our bounds dramatically improve the state of the art. These isogenies in dimension greater than one have become increasingly important in isogeny-based cryptography, and previous works have already conjectured consequences of their expansion properties. We present several applications of our result: we transform conjectural predecessors into rigorous algorithms, and we give the first algorithm for computing endomorphism rings of superspecial principally polarized abelian varieties in arbitrary dimension, with complexity $\tilde O(p^{g-1})$.
papers.authors: Maria Corte-Real Santos, Harun Kır, Olivier Taïbi, Benjamin Wesolowski

papers.title: RM-KLPT: Algebraic Pathfinding for Superspecial Abelian Surfaces with Maximal Real Multiplication
papers.abstract: The isogeny graphs of superspecial abelian surfaces with maximal real multiplication were first studied by Charles, Goren, and Lauter in 2009, when they constructed the RM-CGL hash function on these graphs and proved that they are Ramanujan. As a consequence, these graphs enjoy optimal expansion properties, which are either absent or difficult to establish in other higher-dimensional isogeny graphs. In this paper, we take a closer look at these graphs from a cryptographic perspective, and attempt to demonstrate that they are the natural generalization of the supersingular $\ell$-isogeny graph to dimension two.
